body:
What reliable electricity supply means

An electricity system is reliable when it can deliver electricity to consumers with an acceptable degree of continuity and quality. Reliability depends on having adequate generation, a functioning transmission network, dependable distribution equipment and effective system operation.

Reliability is not the same as installed generating capacity. A region may have substantial generating capacity but still experience interruptions because a transmission line, substation, local feeder or transformer is unavailable.

Major reasons for interruptions

  • Generation shortage: available generating power is insufficient to meet demand.
  • Transmission constraint: enough electricity may exist elsewhere, but the network cannot transfer the required power safely.
  • Equipment failure: a line, breaker, transformer or other network component fails.
  • External disturbance: lightning, storms, falling trees, floods or accidental contact damages the network.
  • Planned interruption: a part of the network is deliberately taken out of service for approved maintenance or other work.

Faults, protection and restoration

An electrical fault may produce abnormal current or voltage conditions. Protection systems detect specified abnormal conditions and direct circuit breakers to disconnect the affected equipment. Isolating a faulty section helps protect people, equipment and the wider grid.

Once a faulted section is isolated, operators may restore unaffected portions through available alternative supply arrangements. Repairs, inspections and safe testing may be necessary before the faulted section is returned to service.

Redundancy means having alternative equipment or pathways capable of performing a necessary function if another component fails. It can improve reliability, but only if the alternatives have sufficient capacity and are themselves available.

System adequacy and operating security

Adequacy concerns whether enough resources and network capacity exist to meet expected demand, including under reasonably foreseeable conditions. Security concerns the ability of an operating system to withstand disturbances and remain stable.

For example, sufficient generating capacity may provide adequacy, but protection failures or an important line outage can still threaten operating security. Both are necessary for dependable electricity supply.

Measuring consumer interruptions

Electricity distribution performance is commonly assessed using interruption indices:

IndexFull nameWhat it measures
SAIFISystem Average Interruption Frequency IndexAverage number of qualifying sustained interruptions experienced per consumer during the reporting period.
SAIDISystem Average Interruption Duration IndexAverage total duration of qualifying sustained interruptions per consumer during the reporting period.

The treatment of planned interruptions, exceptional events and minimum interruption duration depends on the applicable reporting rules. The basic distinction remains: SAIFI measures how often, while SAIDI measures how long.

Continuity and power quality

Continuous supply is one aspect of electricity service. Power quality also concerns matters such as voltage levels, voltage fluctuations, frequency and waveform distortion. Equipment may malfunction even when electricity has not been completely interrupted. A local voltage problem and a system-wide generation-demand imbalance therefore require different explanations.

Prelims focus

  • Generation adequacy does not guarantee uninterrupted distribution supply.
  • Protection systems help isolate faulty equipment.
  • Redundancy can provide an alternative supply path when adequate capacity exists.
  • SAIFI measures interruption frequency; SAIDI measures interruption duration.
  • Planned maintenance outages and unexpected fault outages are different categories.
  • Trap: A local distribution fault need not indicate a shortage of electricity generation.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 7, Electric Current and Its Effects, printed pp. 165–167, sections on heating effects and fuses; Central Electricity Authority, Compendium of Regulations, 2024, reliability-index reporting format; Gujarat Electricity Regulatory Commission, Standards of Performance of Distribution Licensee Regulations, Chapter VII, reliability indices; International Energy Agency, Energy Transitions Require Innovation in Power System Planning, discussion of adequacy, consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Reliability, Electricity Outages and Quality of Supply

body:
Why generated electricity does not all reach consumers

Some electricity produced by a power station is consumed by equipment inside the station itself, such as pumps and fans. Additional energy is lost as electricity travels through transmission lines, transformers and distribution equipment. Consequently, the electricity available at consumer meters is less than the total electricity generated.

It is important to distinguish station auxiliary consumption from transmission and distribution losses. Auxiliary consumption takes place within the generating station; transmission and distribution losses arise in the network.

Technical losses

Technical losses occur because electrical equipment and conductors are not perfectly efficient. The principal example is resistive heating in lines, cables and windings. Transformers and other equipment also have operating losses.

Technical losses can be reduced through appropriate network improvements, better equipment, improved operating practices and reduced overloading. They cannot normally be reduced to absolute zero in a real system.

Commercial losses and revenue collection

Commercial losses arise from failures to measure, bill or collect the value of supplied electricity correctly. Examples include electricity theft, defective or bypassed meters, inaccurate billing and unpaid bills.

Unpaid bills do not mean that additional electrical energy physically disappeared from the wires. They represent a failure to recover revenue. This distinction is central to understanding the term Aggregate Technical and Commercial (AT&C) losses.

CategoryIllustrationNature of the problem
Technical lossHeat produced in a distribution conductor.Physical energy dissipation.
Metering or billing lossEnergy is supplied but not fully recorded or billed.Failure to account for supplied energy.
Collection lossA consumer does not pay the full billed amount.Revenue is not recovered.

How AT&C losses are calculated

The official methodology uses 2 ratios:

  • Billing efficiency: energy billed or sold divided by energy input into the distribution area.
  • Collection efficiency: revenue collected, excluding arrears, divided by the amount billed; under the cited methodology, if arrears cannot be separated, any calculated efficiency above 100% is capped at 100%.

When these efficiencies are expressed as fractions, the calculation is:

AT&C loss percentage = [1 − (Billing efficiency × Collection efficiency)] × 100.

Worked illustration

A distribution area receives 100 kWh and correctly accounts for 85 kWh as billed energy. Its billing efficiency is 85%. Suppose it collects 90% of the amount billed. Its collection efficiency is 90%.

AT&C loss = [1 − (0.85 × 0.90)] × 100 = 23.5%.

The result is a combined technical-and-commercial performance measure. It does not mean that 23.5 kWh of electricity was physically lost in the wires.

Why energy accounting matters

Utilities compare measured electricity input with electricity supplied or billed at successive network levels. Feeder meters, distribution-transformer meters and consumer meters can help locate abnormal losses. Better metering, timely billing, collection and theft prevention address different causes and therefore should not be confused with improving conductor efficiency.

Prelims focus

  • Station auxiliary consumption is separate from transmission and distribution losses.
  • Resistive heating is a technical loss.
  • Theft, underbilling and non-payment contribute to commercial performance problems.
  • AT&C stands for Aggregate Technical and Commercial.
  • AT&C losses depend on both billing efficiency and collection efficiency.
  • Trap: AT&C loss percentage is not the same as the percentage of electricity physically dissipated in the network.

[Sources: NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Infrastructure, Chapter 8, printed pp. 147–148, discussion of net electricity availability and power-sector losses; Power Finance Corporation, Ministry of Power, Methodology for Establishing Baseline AT&C Losses, 4 September 2009, sections 4.3–4.5, printed pp. 8–9.]

pictures.alt: Billing efficiency of 85% combines with money collection efficiency of 90% to give AT&C loss of 23.5%, which is not physical energy loss.
pictures.caption: How billing and collection efficiencies combine into AT&C loss.

title: Electricity Losses: Technical, Commercial and AT&C Losses

body:
Why electricity requires specialised institutions

Generation, power transmission, electricity distribution, grid operation and tariff regulation involve different responsibilities. An institution that determines electricity tariffs is not necessarily the organisation that generates electricity or operates transmission lines.

The Electricity Act, 2003 provides the principal statutory framework for India's electricity sector. It assigns different functions to the Central Electricity Authority, regulatory commissions and load despatch centres.

Important national and state institutions

InstitutionMain responsibilityRelevant legal provision
Central Electricity Authority (CEA)Technical advice, electricity planning, technical standards and sector information.Electricity Act, 2003, Section 73.
Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC)Regulates inter-state transmission and specified central or multi-state generation tariffs and electricity-market matters.Section 79.
State Electricity Regulatory Commission (SERC)Regulates intrastate tariffs, distribution-licensee procurement and other state-level regulatory matters.Section 86.
State Load Despatch Centre (SLDC)Coordinates secure and economic real-time grid operation and scheduling within a state.Section 32.

CEA and CERC are different bodies. CEA has primarily technical, planning and advisory functions, while CERC is an independent electricity regulator exercising the powers specified by law.

How electricity is bought and sold

A generating company may sell electricity through a power purchase agreement (PPA) or through permitted market arrangements. A distribution company, commonly called a DISCOM, procures electricity and supplies consumers in its licensed area.

Wholesale electricity transactions may take different forms:

  • Longer-term contractual purchase: electricity is bought under an agreement specifying commercial and operational terms.
  • Day-ahead market: electricity is traded in advance for delivery during the following day.
  • Real-time market: permitted transactions address electricity requirements closer to actual delivery.

India's regulated power exchanges provide organised platforms for eligible electricity transactions. The CERC Power Market Regulations, 2021, govern specified electricity-market activities, including different contract types and their scheduling requirements.

Electricity trading does not replace grid operation

A commercial contract establishes agreed rights and obligations to buy or sell electricity. However, the physical delivery still requires an available network and approved scheduling under the applicable grid rules. Transmission constraints and system-security requirements can restrict a transaction.

Open access permits eligible participants to use transmission or distribution networks for electricity transactions, subject to applicable regulatory conditions and charges. It does not mean electricity can be carried through another utility's network without payment or operational approval.

Who determines consumer tariffs?

Retail electricity tariffs are generally determined or regulated by the appropriate state electricity regulatory commission under the applicable law and tariff framework. Wholesale market prices, transmission charges and retail tariffs are not identical. A change in the market price for a particular trading period does not automatically make every household's retail tariff change by the same amount.

For example, Gujarat's regulatory commission is the Gujarat Electricity Regulatory Commission (GERC). Its state-level jurisdiction must not be confused with CERC's inter-state regulatory responsibilities.

Prelims focus

  • Electricity Act, 2003: CEA technical functions under Section 73.
  • CERC's functions are specified in Section 79.
  • SERC functions are specified in Section 86.
  • SLDC functions are specified in Section 32.
  • A PPA is a commercial electricity-purchase arrangement; a power exchange is an organised trading platform.
  • Trap: The electricity regulator determines or regulates specified tariffs; it does not itself serve as the grid's real-time dispatch operator.

[Sources: Electricity Act, 2003, Sections 32, 73, 79 and 86; Central Electricity Authority, Functions; Central Electricity Regulatory Commission, Functions (Mandate); CERC, Power Market Regulations, 2021, provisions on day-ahead and real-time contracts; GRID-INDIA, About Grid-India, consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Separate flows show commercial electricity contracts and physical network delivery, with load despatch coordination and regulatory oversight.
pictures.caption: Electricity transactions and physical electricity delivery are different processes.

title: India's Electricity Institutions, Regulation and Power Markets

body:
Restructuring of the Gujarat Electricity Board

Gujarat provides a useful example of how electricity-sector functions are divided among specialised organisations. The former Gujarat Electricity Board (GEB) was restructured with effect from 1 April 2005, separating generation, transmission, distribution and holding-company functions.

The restructuring established a group of state electricity companies with distinct operating responsibilities. Their names are particularly important because several abbreviations appear similar but refer to different functions.

Major state electricity companies

AbbreviationFull namePrincipal role
GSECLGujarat State Electricity Corporation LimitedElectricity generation.
GETCOGujarat Energy Transmission Corporation LimitedState transmission-network functions.
GUVNLGujarat Urja Vikas Nigam LimitedHolding-company functions and bulk electricity procurement arrangements.
DGVCLDakshin Gujarat Vij Company LimitedState-owned distribution utility in southern Gujarat.
MGVCLMadhya Gujarat Vij Company LimitedState-owned distribution utility in central Gujarat.
PGVCLPaschim Gujarat Vij Company LimitedState-owned distribution utility in western Gujarat.
UGVCLUttar Gujarat Vij Company LimitedState-owned distribution utility in northern Gujarat.

These are the 4 principal state-owned regional distribution companies. They are not the only possible electricity-distribution licensees in Gujarat: other licensees, including Torrent Power, serve specified licensed areas. Distribution responsibilities must therefore be identified by the actual licensed supply area.

Grid operation and regulation in Gujarat

Gujarat's State Load Despatch Centre (SLDC) coordinates state-level scheduling and real-time electricity-system operation. The transmission assets and SLDC-related assets of the former GEB were transferred to GETCO as part of the 2005 restructuring, as documented in GERC's March 2022 tariff order. The statutory function of an SLDC is distinct from the business of electricity trading.

GERC performs state electricity-regulatory functions, including tariff determination and regulation of distribution-licensee procurement within its legal jurisdiction. It was constituted in 1998, before the 2005 restructuring of GEB.

Energy efficiency in Gujarat

The Gujarat Energy Development Agency (GEDA) is identified by the national Bureau of Energy Efficiency as Gujarat's State Designated Agency for implementation of provisions of the Energy Conservation Act, 2001.

Thus, the responsibility for promoting energy efficiency must not be confused with the separate responsibilities of GSECL, GETCO, a DISCOM or GERC. A state may need all these organisations to coordinate in practice, but their legal and functional roles remain different.

Application to Gujarat's electricity network

Electricity generated at a conventional or renewable generating station may enter Gujarat's grid, be transmitted through major substations and subsequently reach residential, agricultural, commercial or industrial consumers through the applicable distribution arrangements.

Gujarat's substantial industrial activity, agricultural pumping needs and development of renewable electricity make efficient motors, pumps, building cooling, demand forecasting and reliable network operation important applications of the concepts studied in this lesson.

The institutional structure described here reflects the 2005 restructuring and the cited regulatory documents available by the content cutoff of 15 October 2026. Individual tariffs, licensing areas and operational arrangements should always be read with the date of their governing order.

Prelims focus

  • GEB restructuring took effect on 1 April 2005.
  • GSECL: generation; GETCO: transmission; GUVNL: holding company and bulk procurement.
  • DGVCL, MGVCL, PGVCL and UGVCL are the 4 principal state-owned regional DISCOMs.
  • GERC is Gujarat's state electricity regulator.
  • GEDA is Gujarat's State Designated Agency under the energy-efficiency framework.
  • Trap: GETCO is a transmission company, not one of the 4 regional electricity distribution companies.

[Sources: Gujarat Electricity Regulatory Commission, GETCO Tariff Order for FY 2022–23, March 2022, Background and Brief History, printed p. 2, historical restructuring information; Gujarat Electricity Regulatory Commission, press note dated 25 March 2026 concerning FY 2026–27 distribution tariffs and licensees; Bureau of Energy Efficiency, State Designated Agencies, Gujarat entry, updated 13 April 2026 and consulted 16 November 2026.]
